{"text":"Role: Act as a Senior Product Designer specializing in Premium Fintech SaaS. Task: Create a comprehensive, high-fidelity design system and UI Kit for "Model My Retirement," a sophisticated financial projection platform.

1. Visual Art Direction & Brand
Aesthetic: Premium, trustworthy, and data-dense but clean (High-end Finance: Vanguard/Bloomberg meets modern SaaS).

Primary Palette: Deep Navy (#0F2847), Vibrant Teal (#00a3e0), and Gold Accents (#d4a574).

Surface: Use a "Premium Dark" theme (#0d1117 background, #161b22 cards) and a "Cool Light" theme (#f8fafb background, white cards).

Atmosphere: Subtle gradients (Navy to Teal), frosted glass overlays, and soft, multi-layered shadows for depth.

Typography: Use Inter for UI and a Monospace font (Fira Code) for all numerical financial data.

2. Core Component Library (Create Variants)
Generate the following with Auto Layout, Light/Dark modes, and Mobile/Desktop versions:

Navigation: Vertical sidebar with collapsible sections and active-state teal gradients. Top header with search and user profile.

Data Entry: Floating label inputs, currency-formatted fields (prefix $), and sleek toggle switches.

Financial Cards: * Asset Cards: Value, % growth, and a 6-month sparkline trend.

Liability Cards: Balance, payoff progress bar, and interest rate badges.

KPI Cards: Large Hero stats for Net Worth with comparison subtext.

Data Viz: High-fidelity Chart.js style containers (Line, Bar, Monte Carlo Bell Curves) with legends and tooltip hover states.

Tables: Professional density, zebra-striped, with sortable headers and batch-action checkboxes.

3. Key Page Templates to Generate
Main Dashboard: A 3-column grid showing Net Worth projection hero, asset breakdown, and recent activity.

What-If Scenario Tool: A split-screen comparison view with parameter sliders on the left and real-time updating charts on the right.

Projection Table: A data-heavy multi-level table showing a 20-year financial horizon.

Onboarding/Auth: A premium login page with a Navy-Teal gradient background and a centered glassmorphism card.

4. Technical Constraints
Grid: 8px base spacing system.

Corner Radius: 6px (small), 12px (modals), 16px (hero sections).

Compliance: Ensure WCAG 2.1 contrast and visible focus rings (3px Teal glow)."}

1. I need to create a full design system with theme tokens
2. Build a comprehensive component library
3. Create multiple page templates
4. Support both light and dark themes
5. Use Inter for UI text and Fira Code for financial numbers

- `/src/styles/theme.css` - Update with design tokens
- `/src/app/components/theme-provider.tsx` - Theme context


- Navigation and layout components like a sidebar and header
- Financial display components including KPI cards, asset and liability cards with sparkline charts
- A professional data table component and chart container for visualizations
- Form inputs with floating labels, toggle switches, and the main dashboard page
- A scenario planning tool, 20-year projection table, authentication page, and the root app component with routing

compression.summaryText:
## Background
I'm building "Model My Retirement," a premium fintech SaaS financial projection platform with a design system inspired by Vanguard/Bloomberg meets modern SaaS. The brand palette uses Deep Navy (#0F2847), Vibrant Teal (#00a3e0), and Gold Accents (#d4a574), with dual themes: "Premium Dark" (#0d1117 background, #161b22 cards) and "Cool Light" (#f8fafb background, white cards). Typography uses Inter for UI and Fira Code (monospace) for all financial numerals, with an 8px base spacing grid, specific corner radii (6px/12px/16px), and WCAG 2.1 compliance including 3px teal glow focus rings. The app uses React with Tailwind CSS v4 (CSS-based theme tokens in `@theme inline`), recharts for data visualization, and Lucide icons.

## Current state
The full design system and UI kit are implemented and functional, including: a theme provider with light/dark toggle (`theme-provider.tsx`), collapsible sidebar navigation (`nav-sidebar.tsx`), app header with search (`app-header.tsx`), reusable components (KPI cards, asset cards with SVG sparklines, liability cards with progress bars, floating-label currency inputs, toggle switches), and four complete page templates — a 3-column dashboard (`dashboard-page.tsx`), a split-screen What-If Scenario tool with Monte Carlo bell curves (`scenario-page.tsx`), a 20-year projection table with sortable headers and batch actions (`projections-page.tsx`), and a glassmorphism auth/login page (`auth-page.tsx`). All pages are wired together in `App.tsx` with tab-based navigation and everything renders with mock data — no backend or real API integration exists yet.

## Background
I'm building "Model My Retirement," a premium fintech SaaS financial projection platform with a design system inspired by Vanguard/Bloomberg meets modern SaaS. The brand palette uses Deep Navy (#0F2847), Vibrant Teal (#00a3e0), and Gold Accents (#d4a574), with dual themes: "Premium Dark" (#0d1117 background, #161b22 cards) and "Cool Light" (#f8fafb background, white cards). Typography uses Inter for UI and Fira Code (monospace) for all financial numerals, with an 8px base spacing grid, specific corner radii (6px/12px/16px), and WCAG 2.1 compliance including 3px teal glow focus rings. The app uses React with Tailwind CSS v4 (CSS-based theme tokens in `@theme inline`), recharts for data visualization, and Lucide icons.

## Current state
The full design system and UI kit are implemented and functional, including a complete theme provider, navigation components, reusable UI components, and four complete page templates with mock data. I just fixed a Tailwind CSS v4 error where `font-ui` and `font-mono` utility classes weren't being recognized due to incorrect variable naming in the `@theme inline` block — changed `--font-family-ui` to `--font-ui` and `--font-family-mono` to `--font-mono` to properly generate the font utilities.

## Background
I'm building "Model My Retirement," a premium fintech SaaS financial projection platform with a design system inspired by Vanguard/Bloomberg meets modern SaaS. The brand palette uses Deep Navy (#0F2847), Vibrant Teal (#00a3e0), and Gold Accents (#d4a574), with dual themes: "Premium Dark" (#0d1117 background, #161b22 cards) and "Cool Light" (#f8fafb background, white cards). Typography uses Inter for UI and Fira Code (monospace) for all financial numerals, with an 8px base spacing grid, specific corner radii (6px/12px/16px), and WCAG 2.1 compliance including 3px teal glow focus rings. The app uses React with Tailwind CSS v4 (CSS-based theme tokens in `@theme inline`), recharts for data visualization, and Lucide icons. The full design system and UI kit are implemented including a theme provider, navigation components (sidebar in `nav-sidebar.tsx`, header in `app-header.tsx`), reusable UI components (shadcn-style in `/src/app/components/ui/`), and four complete page templates: dashboard (`dashboard-page.tsx`), scenario modeling (`scenario-page.tsx`), projections (`projections-page.tsx`), and auth (`auth-page.tsx`), all with mock data.

## Current state
The app is fully functional with no build errors. The last assistant fixed two minor issues: added `relative` positioning to sidebar nav buttons so the active indicator positions correctly, and corrected a non-standard Tailwind opacity value (`/8` → `/[8%]`) on the KPI card's gold background decoration in `kpi-card.tsx`.

{"text":"The user wants me to build a comprehensive Design System page/showcase that demonstrates all the reusable components in their "Model My Retirement" application. They want to keep the current app as-is and create a new page that serves as a living design system reference — something they can use to see all available components, their variants, states, and usage patterns.

Let me plan this out:

1. Create a new `DesignSystemPage` component that showcases:
   - Typography system (headings, body text, monospace numerals)
   - Color palette (brand colors, semantic colors, theme tokens)
   - Spacing & Grid system
   - Buttons (all variants, sizes, states)
   - Cards (KPI cards, asset cards, liability cards, info cards)
   - Form inputs (floating inputs, toggles, selects, search)
   - Data visualization (sparklines, chart examples)
   - Badges & Tags
   - Navigation elements
   - Layout patterns
   - Icons

2. Add "Design System" to the navigation sidebar
3. Wire it up in App.tsx

I'll build this comprehensively as a new component and integrate it into the nav and App.tsx. I need to showcase typography with the font families used (Inter for UI, Fira Code for numerals), then move through the color palette, spacing system, and all the interactive components with their various states and variants. I'm adding data display components like sparklines, badges, progress bars, and tables, plus layout foundations for spacing and shadows. Then I'll create a new design system page component, wire it into the navigation sidebar, and integrate it into the main app.","signature":""}

## Background
I'm building "Model My Retirement," a premium fintech SaaS financial projection platform with a design system inspired by Vanguard/Bloomberg meets modern SaaS. The brand palette uses Deep Navy (#0F2847), Vibrant Teal (#00a3e0), and Gold Accents (#d4a574), with dual themes: "Premium Dark" (#0d1117 background, #161b22 cards) and "Cool Light" (#f8fafb background, white cards). Typography uses Inter for UI and Fira Code (monospace) for all financial numerals, with an 8px base spacing grid, specific corner radii (6px/12px/16px), and WCAG 2.1 compliance including 3px teal glow focus rings. The app uses React with Tailwind CSS v4 (CSS-based theme tokens in `@theme inline`), recharts for data visualization, Lucide icons, and shadcn-style reusable UI components in `/src/app/components/ui/`. The full UI kit includes a theme provider, navigation components (sidebar in `nav-sidebar.tsx`, header in `app-header.tsx`), and five page templates: dashboard (`dashboard-page.tsx`), scenario modeling (`scenario-page.tsx`), projections (`projections-page.tsx`), auth (`auth-page.tsx`), and a comprehensive design system reference (`design-system-page.tsx`), all with mock data. The design system page is intended to serve as a reference I can use alongside regular Figma design files.

## Current state
The app is fully functional with no build errors. The latest addition is a comprehensive Design System reference page (`/src/app/components/design-system-page.tsx`) accessible via a "Design System" link under a new "System" section in the sidebar navigation — it documents 13 sections (color palette, typography, spacing/radii, shadows/elevation, buttons, form controls, cards, badges/tags, data display, charts, feedback/alerts, navigation patterns, and accessibility) with a collapsible table of contents and click-to-copy tokens, using inline styles for dynamically-generated chart color swatches to avoid Tailwind scanning issues.

## Background
I'm building "Model My Retirement," a premium fintech SaaS financial projection platform with a design system inspired by Vanguard/Bloomberg meets modern SaaS. The brand palette uses Deep Navy (#0F2847), Vibrant Teal (#00a3e0), and Gold Accents (#d4a574), with dual themes: "Premium Dark" (#0d1117 background, #161b22 cards) and "Cool Light" (#f8fafb background, white cards). Typography uses Inter for UI and Fira Code (monospace) for all financial numerals, with an 8px base spacing grid, specific corner radii (6px/12px/16px), and WCAG 2.1 compliance including 3px teal glow focus rings. The app uses React with Tailwind CSS v4 (CSS-based theme tokens in `@theme inline`), recharts for data visualization, Lucide icons, and shadcn-style reusable UI components in `/src/app/components/ui/`. The full UI kit includes a theme provider, navigation components (sidebar in `nav-sidebar.tsx`, header in `app-header.tsx`), and five page templates: dashboard (`dashboard-page.tsx`), scenario modeling (`scenario-page.tsx`), projections (`projections-page.tsx`), auth (`auth-page.tsx`), and a comprehensive design system reference (`design-system-page.tsx`), all with mock data. The design system page documents 13 sections with a collapsible table of contents and click-to-copy tokens, using inline styles for dynamically-generated chart color swatches to avoid Tailwind scanning issues. It's accessible via a "Design System" link under a "System" section in the sidebar.

## Current state
The app is fully functional with no build errors, but currently uses state-based routing (`useState` in `App.tsx`) rather than URL-based routing — there's no `react-router-dom` installed, so browser back/forward and bookmarkable URLs aren't supported. I've asked the assistant to help me "enable pages" (set up proper routing and build out placeholder pages), and they audited the project and presented me with options: (1) installing `react-router-dom` for real URL routing, (2) choosing which of the 9 placeholder pages to build out (Portfolio: Investments, Real Estate, Retirement Accounts, Mortgage, Loans, Income Streams; Planning: Retirement Goals, Insurance, Tax Strategy), (3) deciding on page depth (full-featured vs. solid starter), and (4) whether to add a Settings page — but I haven't yet answered any of these questions, so the next assistant should re-present these options or ask me for my preferences before proceeding.

{"text":"The user wants:
1. URL routing with react-router-dom
2. All 9 placeholder pages built out
3. Full-featured pages
4. Settings page too

That's a massive undertaking. Let me plan this carefully:

**Pages to build (10 new pages):**
1. Assets - Investments (`/portfolio/assets/investments`)
2. Assets - Real Estate (`/portfolio/assets/real-estate`)
3. Assets - Retirement Accounts (`/portfolio/assets/retirement`)
4. Liabilities - Mortgage (`/portfolio/liabilities/mortgage`)
5. Liabilities - Loans (`/portfolio/liabilities/loans`)
6. Income Streams (`/portfolio/income`)


7. Retirement Goals (`/planning/goals`)
8. Insurance (`/planning/insurance`)
9. Tax Strategy (`/planning/tax`)
10. Settings (`/settings`)

**Existing pages to keep:**
- Auth (`/auth` or `/login`)
- Dashboard (`/dashboard` or `/`)
- Scenario (`/scenarios`)
- Projections (`/projections`)
- Design System (`/design-system`)

**Routing structure:**
```
/ → redirect to /dashboard
/dashboard
/scenarios
/projections
/portfolio/assets/investments
/portfolio/assets/real-estate
/portfolio/assets/retirement
/portfolio/liabilities/mortgage
/portfolio/liabilities/loans
/portfolio/income
/planning/goals
/planning/insurance
/planning/tax
/settings
/auth
/design-system
```

Now I'll install react-router-dom and build out all the pages. Each one needs KPI cards at the top, a main content area with tables or charts, action buttons for adding and editing, and mock data using the design system components. I'll start with the router setup, then create each page file systematically, and finally update the App and navigation components to wire everything together. TD Return, Dividend Yield, Asset Count with a holdings table showing stock details, allocation donut chart, and options to add investments or export data. For real estate, I'm planning KPI cards for property value and equity alongside property cards with mortgage details and a value trend chart. The retirement accounts section will display total balances, contribution limits, and a growth projection with a contribution breakdown and RMD calculator. I'm also mapping out mortgage, loans, and income pages with their respective KPI cards, detailed tables, and comparison tools like debt payoff strategies. Finishing up the tax page with KPI cards for tax liability, deferred balances, and Roth conversions, plus tools for tax-loss harvesting and RMD planning. The settings page will handle profile management, preferences, notifications, and account security. This is going to require a lot of component files, so I need to stay focused and efficient with each one. I'm also planning the router setup using react-router-dom v6 with BrowserRouter, and I'll need to update the nav-sidebar to use the navigation hooks instead of callbacks.

I'm deciding between refactoring NavSidebar to use `useNavigate` and `useLocation` directly, or keeping it prop-based and deriving the active page from the URL in the main App component. The cleaner approach is to have NavSidebar handle its own routing logic with the hooks. Now I need to map out how the nav IDs correspond to the actual routes so everything connects properly.

Given the scope of creating 10 full pages plus routing infrastructure, I should be strategic about this: install react-router-dom, scaffold all the page files, refactor App.tsx with the router setup, then update NavSidebar to use the router hooks. I'll keep each page substantive but focused. Let me start implementing this systematically, beginning with the router configuration using BrowserRouter. Now I'm planning the page structure—each one will have KPIs at the top, a grid of charts and tables in the middle, and action buttons, all built with the existing design components. I'll refactor the NavSidebar to use React Router hooks internally instead of the callback props, keeping the collapse state separate, and update App.tsx to wire everything together with the router. Now I'm setting up the routing structure with a config object that maps paths to page metadata like titles and subtitles, and updating the nav items to include path properties so the sidebar can track the active route. I'll start implementing all the code, beginning with the package installation and then building out each page with a consistent structure of imports, mock data, and a component that displays KPIs alongside the main content. and then proceed to create each file.

Actually wait - I need to think about this more carefully. Creating 10 full-featured pages in one go is a LOT of code. Let me estimate:
- Each full-featured page: ~200-400 lines
- That's 2000-4000 lines of new code
- Plus refactoring existing files

Let me be smart about this and create rich, well-designed pages that aren't unnecessarily verbose. I'll use the existing component library (KpiCard, AssetCard, LiabilityCard, FloatingInput, ToggleSwitch, Sparkline) throughout to keep things consistent and reduce code duplication.

Let me start now.

First, let me plan the exact structure of each page. The Investments page will have KPIs for total value, YTD return, dividend yield, and holdings count, along with a sortable holdings table, sector allocation chart, recent dividends list, and an add investment button. Real Estate needs property value and equity KPIs, property cards, an appreciation chart, and a form to add properties. Retirement Accounts will display total balance, contribution limits, employer match, and projected balance at 65, with account breakdown cards, contribution progress bars, growth projections, and an RMD table. The Mortgage page will show balance, monthly payment, and other key metrics.

I'm continuing to map out the remaining pages - Loans, Income, and Goals - each with their own KPIs, visualizations, and interactive elements. This is a comprehensive financial dashboard that ties together all the user's assets, liabilities, and financial goals.

Now I'm adding the Insurance and Tax Strategy pages with their specific metrics and analysis tools, then moving into Settings for user preferences and data management. I'm ready to start building out all these components.

For the router setup, I need to decide between `BrowserRouter` and `HashRouter` for this Vite + React project. Since it's a single-page app in Figma Make, `HashRouter` would be safer to avoid server routing issues, but `BrowserRouter` is the standard approach and should work fine here too. I'll go with `BrowserRouter` for now.

Now I'm ready to start building out the files. My plan is to install react-router-dom, set up the route configuration, create all 10 page components with realistic mock data (aiming for 200-300 lines each to keep them feature-rich), then update the navigation and main App component to wire everything together. I'll start with the investments page since it needs a solid holdings table with mock data.

Actually, I need to think through the architecture first. The NavSidebar currently uses `activePage` and `onNavigate` callbacks, so I have to decide whether to couple it directly to react-router or keep it decoupled with prop drilling. I'll go with direct router integration since it's cleaner for a real app. That means I need to add a `path` field to each nav item to map IDs to routes, and I'll need to handle how parent items like "assets" and "liabilities" work with routing when they currently just toggle expand states.

Looking at the existing click handler, parent items toggle the section while leaf items navigate, which is the behavior I want to keep. I'll just swap out the `onNavigate` call for react-router's `navigate()` function and use `useLocation().pathname` to determine which item is currently active. Now I'm setting up the path mapping for the nav sections...

Defining the nav structure... Continuing to structure the navigation menu...

Now I need to figure out how to determine when a parent item should appear active based on its children's routes. I'll check if the current pathname matches the parent's route prefix—so any path under `/portfolio/assets/` activates the assets parent, and similarly for liabilities under `/portfolio/liabilities/`.

I could add a `pathPrefix` property to parent items, but actually it's simpler to just check if any child's path matches the current location. If there's a match, the parent becomes active and expands.

For the AppHeader, instead of hardcoding title and subtitle, I'll derive them from the current route in App.tsx using a route config that maps paths to metadata. This keeps AppHeader decoupled and reusable.

My implementation plan: install react-router-dom, create all the page components, then update the navigation structure to support routing.

Now I'm checking if app-header needs any changes to work with the routing setup.
